 The teleconverter is the weirdest smartphone trend right now
 Opinion 
 Nov 2, 2026 
 News of Honor's latest camera accessory offering marks an ongoing smartphone trend that leaves me a little confused 
 Credit: Foundry | Alex Walker-Todd 
 More and more Chinese smartphone manufacturers are making teleconverter camera accessories for their flagship phones, and I find it all a little odd.
 The imminent Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is set to feature a pretty serious camera system, together with an optional 500mm lens extender. This follows on from a similar accessory for the Honor Magic 8 Pro (pictured).
 Now the company is said to be going even further with this trend by offering a teleconverter for its more mainstream smartphone series.
 Established tipster Digital Chat Station has taken to Weibo to claim that the Honor 700 and Honor 700 Pro will support a 200mm telephoto extender when it launches in China next month.
 Foundry | Alex Walker-Todd
 Ready for your close-up?
 Honor isn’t alone in offering such a provision, of course. Most recently we’ve seen the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max (following on from the Oppo Find X9 Ultra ) giving us a Hasselblad-branded teleconverter kit, producing tack-sharp 10x zoomed shots and enhanced 40x hybrid snaps.
 The Vivo X300 Series, for its part, launched with a Zeiss 400mm telephoto kit option, as did the recent Vivo X500 Pro Max.
 While Xiaomi hasn’t (yet) released its own Leica-assisted lens for its Pro Max or Ultra smartphone line-up, it routinely offers pro photography kits with enhanced physical shooting options.
 The reasoning behind such team-ups seems fairly clear. This is a mature and extremely competitive smartphone market, and the likes of Apple, Google and and even Samsung bring varying degrees of photographic cachet to the table.
 Allying with dedicated camera marques serves as a helpful shortcut for Chinese manufacturers to do more than compete on quality (Oppo and Xiaomi have been among the best in the business for a couple of years now), by breaking through to a high-spending and brand-conscious audience.
 Chris Martin / Foundry
 Ah, snap
 However, I’m not sure that these dedicated teleconverter accessories are what’s going to swing it for such companies. In my experience, these add-ons prove to be impractical in their unwieldiness.
 Does the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max teleconverter take impressively sharp zoomed shots that you can’t get from the regular camera? Yes it does. It also requires a fiddly snap-and-slide installation process, via a special case, that blocks out the other two cameras and requires you to activate a dedicated mode.
 This all feels somewhat counter-intuitive to me. The old adage that ‘the best camera is the one you have with you’ has been proven spectacularly true with the explosion of smartphone photography.
 Adding an extra element into the process – and a particularly heavy and fiddly-to-install one at that – runs counter to that point-and-shoot spirit.
 oplus_8593080320
 Chris Martin / Foundry
 I suspect that the majority of photography enthusiasts who are motivated to spend money and leave pocket space for a dedicated telephoto lens would much sooner apply those precious resources to buying a dedicated camera – or a lens for an existing camera.
 It’s quite possible I’m wrong, and these smartphone teleconverter kits will form an effective gateway drug for a new generation of would-be photographers. If that were to prove to be the case, however, I suspect it would need to be made much more accessible in terms of price and usability.
 Perhaps, then, Honor has the right idea in opening the concept out to its more affordable smartphone range. I remain deeply sceptical, but also interested to see how this curious trend plays out.
